A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RetrievalAttention, with matching core methods, equations, experiments, and appendices. Their complete text, tables, figures, and algorithms are readable and support comparison, including the additional appendices in v3.

before.justification: v1 reports original accuracy experiments on ∞-Bench, RULER, and Needle-in-a-haystack, attention and vector-search analyses, and decoding latency measurements on RTX4090 and A100 hardware.

after.justification: v3 retains original experimental results and adds baseline comparisons, controlled sparsity analysis, retrieval-budget experiments, million-token retrieval accuracy, and a 70B-model evaluation.

M1.justification: The core attention-aware index, CPU–GPU execution, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. Appendix F adds a tested PyramidKV-based variant that changes retrieval-budget allocation across layers, assigning more tokens to lower layers instead of using a uniform budget. This is a limited procedural adaptation, not a replacement of the main method.

E1.justification: The three benchmark suites and their existing tasks remain. Appendix A.3 extends Needle-in-a-haystack accuracy evaluation from the earlier 4K–128K range to 250K–1M tokens, adding an extreme-length retrieval scenario. v1 already measured million-token latency, but did not report retrieval accuracy at those lengths.

E2.justification: v1 explicitly excludes Quest and discusses InfiniGen without evaluating it. v3 adds Quest to the three-model ∞-Bench comparison, InfiniGen to its Llama-3 comparison, and both methods to the appendix RULER comparison in Table 9. Figure 6 also introduces RobustVamana as an OOD-aware index comparator. These substantially expand the evaluated alternatives.

E3.justification: StreamingLLM's budget changes from 640 to 2K tokens in Tables 2–3. Section 2.3 replaces a 64K-token, single-query Llama-2 sparsity examination with a 100K-token Llama-3 experiment profiling 20 generated tokens and comparing static versus dynamic top-1000 selection. New settings include uniform versus layer-dependent retrieval budgets and Llama-3-70B on eight A100 GPUs. Table 1 changes its named model, and Appendix C changes the stated KV precision from FP32 to FP16; these reporting revisions do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 replaces the original attention-score/MSE illustration with a controlled static-versus-dynamic selection analysis across heads and layers. Section 4.4 adds direct recall-versus-scanning analysis of RetrievalAttention and competing indexes across three models. Appendix F adds a layer-budget allocation ablation, and Appendix A.3 adds extreme-context retrieval stress tests. The latency breakdown moved from v1 Appendix A.3 to v3 Section 4.3 is retained evidence, not a new analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed schedules, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new profiling of 20 consecutive generated tokens is an evaluation-design detail, not a report of independent repetitions or uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: The main RetrievalAttention benchmark scores and 0.188-second decoding latency are retained, but substantial results are added or replaced. The new sparsity analysis reports 89% dynamic versus 71% static attention recovery; new results cover additional baselines, million-token retrieval, and budget allocation. Table 11 reports 70B-model accuracy/latency of 23.5%/1.62 seconds for RetrievalAttention versus 24.0%/5.68 seconds for Flat. StreamingLLM's Llama-3 RULER average changes from 15.80 to 25.01 under its larger token budget, so this is not a same-setting gain.

T1.justification: Section 2.3 introduces a mathematical definition of recovery ratio as the cumulative attention weight of the top-k critical tokens, replacing the earlier MSE-based characterization. This is a limited metric definition: the attention approximation and CPU–GPU combination equations (1)–(5) remain unchanged, and no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The central training-free, OOD-aware retrieval contribution and the 4.9×/1.98× decoding-speedup claims remain. The abstract drops the specific claim that serving an 8B model with 128K tokens requires only 16GB of GPU memory, retaining the less specific claim that it fits on a single 24GB RTX4090. This narrows the quantitative memory claim without redefining the contribution.

C2.justification: v3 adds an explanation attributing InfiniGen's accuracy loss to inaccurate speculation from previous layers. Appendix F interprets the budget-allocation results as task dependent, explicitly noting improved KV retrieval but reduced English QA performance. The million-token and 70B experiments extend the applicability discussion, while the central explanation based on dynamic sparsity and query–key distribution mismatch remains.

D1.justification: v3 distinguishes the RTX4090 server's 10 physical CPU cores from its 20 logical cores and newly specifies the A100 testbed's EPYC 7V13 processor and 220GB DRAM. It documents the new 70B experiment's eight 40GB A100 GPUs and layer partitioning. Appendix C revises the stated original KV format from FP32 to FP16 without explaining whether this corrects documentation or reflects an implementation change. Most implementation optimizations were already documented in v1.

R1.justification: v3 adds references covering ANNS applications and algorithms, OOD-DiskANN, PyramidKV, and PQCache. Section 5 extends the comparison with concurrent work to PQCache, while Appendix D narrows the earlier blanket assertion that related sparse-transformer approaches require retraining to acknowledge approaches targeting CPU-only scenarios. The overall research positioning remains intact.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and background receive substantial rewriting and expanded explanations of ANNS operation, distribution mismatch, and resource requirements. The evaluation narrative incorporates the former appendix latency breakdown, adds a dedicated index-analysis subsection, and gains appendices E–G. Citations and references also change from numbered to author–year organization.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a different document template and substantially reorganizes displays. Figure 1 and Table 1 are placed together; the original composite Figure 2 is reworked into separate sparsity and OOD displays; new recall curves and a million-token heatmap appear. Table 2 gains comparator rows, the latency breakdown moves into the main text, and Tables 9–11 add new appendix comparisons. These changes go well beyond renumbering or numerical updates.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation of the central efficiency argument: Figure 6 directly tests the proposed index's recall versus scanning cost, whereas v1's corresponding plots only examined conventional indexes. Quest, InfiniGen, and RobustVamana comparisons address important comparator gaps, and the controlled sparsity and budget analyses improve explanatory support. Million-token accuracy and 70B tests broaden validation. Limits remain: Table 11 shows 23.5% accuracy versus 35.0% for full attention, and the precision/model-reporting revisions are unexplained. Nevertheless, the added evidence resolves substantial weaknesses in v1's experimental support.
